title-group.article-title: Rocky Desertification Sensitivity Changes and Management Zoning in the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site

abstract.p: Identifying changes in rocky desertification sensitivity is an important basis for land degradation prevention and sustainable use in karst World Natural Heritage sites. This study incorporates recent sensitivity deterioration into zoning rules to distinguish prevention and restoration priorities under conservation constraints. Using multisource data for five observation years from 2005 to 2023, we constructed the rocky desertification sensitivity index (RDSI) for the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site. We analysed the spatiotemporal changes and spatial clustering of RDSI and the composition of its dominant sensitivity components. The optimal parameter-based geographical detector then assessed associations with external factors and their interactions. Management zoning integrated 2023 sensitivity classes, class changes from 2020 to 2023, tourism development potential and core zone protection constraints. Sensitivity declined overall, with mean RDSI falling from 4.112 to 3.540 (13.91%), although the direction of change varied among periods. Improvement covered 36.47% of the area from 2015 to 2020, whereas deterioration covered 17.49% from 2020 to 2023. RDSI showed significant spatial clustering in all five years, and types dominated by slope or fractional rock cover predominated. Among external factors, elevation had the highest spatial explanatory power in every year, with a multiyear mean q value of 0.362, followed by land-use intensity and mean annual temperature. Interaction detection showed that the combination of precipitation and elevation had the highest mean joint q value (0.465). The study area was ultimately divided into five management zones, among which conservation maintenance and low disturbance use predominated, accounting for 42.83% and 27.29%, respectively. The remaining areas were assigned to risk prevention, priority restoration, and conservation and use coordination zones. These findings show that declining sensitivity over the long term can coexist with recent localised deterioration. Integrating current sensitivity classes, recent change, tourism development potential and protection constraints helps identify spatial priorities for core zone conservation, field verification of recently deteriorating patches and assessment of restoration needs, and low disturbance use in peripheral areas.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Karst rocky desertification is a process of land degradation arising from interactions among soil loss, vegetation degradation and bedrock exposure in carbonate rock regions. It constrains the sustainable use of land resources and may impair ecosystem functioning [1,2]. Karst regions have shallow, spatially discontinuous soils and close connections between surface water and groundwater. They are sensitive to climate change and land use disturbance [3]. In recent years, ecological restoration and land use adjustments have contributed to an overall reduction in rocky desertification in parts of the karst region of Southwest China, although the direction of change has varied across regions and periods [4,5,6]. In karst World Natural Heritage sites, maintaining ecological and landscape integrity also requires coordination of tourism use in peripheral areas [7,8]. Identifying changes in rocky desertification sensitivity over the long term and recent risks is therefore an important basis for setting priorities for land degradation prevention.

Remote sensing monitoring and spatial assessment provide a basis for identifying environmental changes and differences in risk across karst regions. Studies in karst regions such as Chongqing and Guangxi have identified changes in rocky desertification across periods and their relationships with natural and human factors [5,6]. International karst research has also examined land use change, ecological degradation and conservation management at different scales. Research in Slovenia, in the northwestern Dinaric karst, used imagery from multiple sources to identify land use changes over the long term and recent vegetation disturbance [9]. Research on representative dolines in the same region combined historical records and ecological surveys to analyse human-induced land degradation and its long-term ecological effects [10]. A global comparison of 31 karst World Natural Heritage sites, including Ha Long Bay–Cat Ba Archipelago, assessed threat intensity and its changes, identifying tourism use, construction and development, and inadequate management as key conservation concerns [11]. For sensitivity assessment, the Technical Guidelines for the Delineation of Ecological Red Lines proposed an approach based on the proportion of exposed carbonate rock, slope and fractional vegetation cover [12].

Previous research has further used environmental information to inform ecological restoration and tourism decisions. Research on the Trang An Landscape Complex used palaeoenvironmental and historical evidence to inform ecological restoration and adaptive conservation management [13]. A study of Cat Ba Island compared tourism development scenarios using a system dynamics model and showed that water shortages, pollution and visitor crowding could limit tourism growth [14]. For spatial management, ecological restoration zoning has combined a modified resistance model, ecological network resilience assessment and cluster analysis to identify spatial units requiring priority restoration [15]. Research in protected karst areas has used indices of conservation significance and disturbance to determine management priorities [16]. Participatory multicriteria assessment has combined participatory weighting with the overlay of suitability layers to coordinate nature conservation, tourism and recreation, and community development objectives [17]. Ecotourism functional zoning has integrated ecological sensitivity, tourism resource potential and spatiotemporal changes in human activity through spatial overlay to determine conservation and use directions [18]. These studies determine management directions from restoration needs, conservation priorities and suitability for use, and some also consider spatiotemporal changes in human activity.

Building on these studies, it remains necessary to clarify how recent changes in sensitivity itself can directly inform management categories. Zoning based solely on current sensitivity classes cannot distinguish the management needs of recently deteriorating and non-deteriorating units within the same class. This may overlook early prevention needs in low sensitivity units that have recently deteriorated and leave restoration priorities unclear for recently deteriorating patches with moderate or high sensitivity. Tourism use in peripheral areas of World Heritage sites also depends on conservation requirements and conditions for use. Change direction therefore needs to be incorporated into zoning criteria alongside conservation requirements and conditions for tourism use to determine management priorities.

Guilin Karst forms part of the South China Karst serial World Heritage property and also faces the need to coordinate landscape conservation and tourism use. The World Heritage Committee has emphasised maintaining the integrity of the property, strengthening management across the entire catchment, and preventing tourism, agriculture and urban development from damaging heritage values [19]. Studies of South China Karst heritage sites have examined the ecological impacts of land use, as well as temporal variation and scale dependence in ecosystem services [20,21]. In this context, further work is needed to clarify spatiotemporal changes and recent deterioration in rocky desertification sensitivity, identify the internal components of different sensitivity units and their spatial associations with external environmental factors, and examine how current sensitivity and recent change can inform differentiated management.

To address these questions, this study uses multisource spatial data for five observation years from 2005 to 2023 to construct the rocky desertification sensitivity index (RDSI) for the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site from fractional rock cover, slope and fractional vegetation cover. We analyse its spatiotemporal changes and dominant internal components, and use the optimal parameters-based geographical detector to examine associations with external factors and their interactions [22,23]. We then combine 2023 sensitivity classes, class changes from 2020 to 2023, tourism development potential and core zone protection constraints to delineate five management zones. The main contribution is to translate recent increases in sensitivity class into explicit zoning criteria. Low sensitivity units with recent deterioration are assigned to risk prevention, whereas deteriorating units with moderate or high sensitivity are identified as priorities for field verification and assessment of restoration needs. For areas without deterioration, management direction is further determined from current sensitivity, protection constraints and tourism development potential. This approach can inform spatial priorities for land degradation prevention, verification of restoration needs and low disturbance use in comparable karst protected areas, with specific indicators and decision thresholds adapted to local environmental conditions and conservation requirements.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Area
sec.p: The study area is located in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China, at approximately 24°44′09″ to 25°09′12″ N and 110°18′56″ to 110°34′21″ E. It comprises the Lijiang Gorge cone karst component, the Putao tower karst component, and their surrounding buffer zones (Figure 1), with a total area of approximately 724.319 km2. The core zones cover approximately 256.38 km2 and the buffer zones cover approximately 467.94 km2. Tower karst plains, cone karst depressions, and gorge landforms form an interspersed landscape. Sloping terrain, patches of shallow soil, and exposed bedrock provide the natural setting for rocky desertification sensitivity. Conservation of the World Heritage property is closely connected with tourism services and the livelihoods of nearby residents. Management must therefore maintain the landscape and ecological processes of the property while considering the effects of activities in surrounding areas.

sec.title: 2.2. Data Sources and Preprocessing
sec.p: The study used Landsat imagery for five observation years, a digital elevation model, and spatial data on climate, soil, land use, socioeconomic conditions, and points of interest. Table 1 summarises their sources, applications, processing methods, and native spatial resolutions. All datasets were preprocessed consistently. Landsat imagery for 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2023 was obtained through Google Earth Engine (GEE). Images were selected from 1 January to 31 December of each year. The QA_PIXEL quality control band was used to exclude pixels contaminated by clouds, cloud shadows and similar effects. Valid observations passing the quality screening were composited using an annual pixel-wise median and clipped to the study area boundary to produce annual composite images at a spatial resolution of 30 m. NDVI and NDRI were then calculated through band math in ENVI 5.6.2. All spatial datasets were projected to the WGS 1984 UTM Zone 49N coordinate system. RDSI and the final management zones were represented at a 30 m raster resolution. Driving factors were summarised using regular grids of 250, 500, 750, and 1000 m.

sec.title: 2.3. Rocky Desertification Sensitivity Assessment
sec.p: Following the rocky desertification sensitivity assessment framework in Appendix B of the Technical Guidelines for the Delineation of Ecological Red Lines issued in May 2015, the proportion of exposed carbonate rock, terrain slope, and fractional vegetation cover were selected as assessment components. The normalized difference rock index (NDRI) and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) were calculated to represent the karst surface characteristics of the study area. Fractional rock cover (FRC) [24] and fractional vegetation cover (FVC) [25] were then retrieved using the dimidiate pixel model as follows. (1)NDRI=ρSWIR−ρNIRρSWIR+ρNIR (2)NDVI=ρNIR−ρREDρNIR+ρRED (3)FRC=NDRI−NDRIminNDRImax−NDRImin (4)FVC=NDVI−NDVIminNDVImax−NDVImin where ρSWIR, ρNIR, and ρRED are the reflectance values of the shortwave infrared, near infrared, and red bands, respectively. After calculating NDVI and NDRI, anomalous values below −1 or above 1 were excluded. The lower and upper endmembers of both indices were defined as the 5th and 95th percentiles of valid pixels within the study area for each year. Endmembers were calculated independently for each year rather than held constant across years. Detailed results of the sensitivity test for endmember determination are provided in the Supplementary Materials. The percentile selection for NDVI endmembers followed reference [26], and the same statistical rule was applied to NDRI. The resulting FVC and FRC values were constrained to [0, 1].

Sensitivity scores followed Table B3 in Appendix B of the Technical Guidelines for the Delineation of Ecological Red Lines, with the specific criteria provided in Table 2. RDSI was calculated from the sensitivity scores of the three components using the geometric mean specified in Appendix B.2.3. (5)RDSI=D×P×C3

D, P, and C are the sensitivity scores assigned to FRC, SLP, and FVC, respectively. Following Table B11 in Appendix B.3 of the guidelines, RDSI was divided using thresholds of 2, 4, 6, and 8 into five classes, namely insensitive, slightly sensitive, moderately sensitive, highly sensitive, and extremely sensitive. RDSI therefore represents rocky desertification sensitivity under the selected surface components and scoring rules. It can inform land degradation prevention and management in the World Heritage property, but should not be equated directly with the actual degree of rocky desertification or the state of land degradation.

sec.title: 2.4. Class Transitions and Dominant Sensitivity Components
sec.p: RDSI classes in consecutive observation years were cross tabulated following the transition analysis method for classified maps [27]. Five class transition matrices were constructed to calculate the areas and proportions that remained within the same class or shifted between classes. The main transition pathways were displayed using Sankey diagrams. The change value was defined as the earlier class code minus the later class code. Positive, negative, and zero values indicate decreasing sensitivity, increasing sensitivity, and no crossing of a class boundary, respectively.

To reveal differences in component composition within the same RDSI class, classification rules were developed from the maximum assigned score and ties, drawing on approaches for identifying limiting ecological sensitivity components [28]. The dominant sensitivity component of each pixel was determined by comparing the assigned scores for FRC, SLP, and FVC. A component with a unique maximum score was classified as singly dominant. Ties between two components were assigned to the corresponding codominant type. Pixels with equal scores for all three components were classified as jointly dominated when the score exceeded 1 and as joint low sensitivity when all three scores equalled 1.

sec.title: 2.5. Spatial Autocorrelation Analysis
sec.p: Global and local spatial autocorrelation analyses were used to characterise the overall spatial association and local clustering of RDSI [29,30]. Global Moran’s I measured overall spatial autocorrelation in RDSI, while local Moran’s I was used to construct maps of local indicators of spatial association (LISA) and identify clusters of high or low values and spatial outliers. The statistics were calculated as follows. (6)I=nS0∑i=1n∑j=1nwijxi−x¯xj−x¯∑i=1nxi−x¯2 (7)Ii=xi−x¯m2∑j=1nwijxj−x¯ where n is the number of spatial units included in the analysis. xi and xj are the RDSI values of units i and j, respectively, x¯ is the mean RDSI for the corresponding year, and wij is the spatial weight. S0=∑i∑jwij is the sum of all spatial weights, and m2=∑ixi−x¯2n is the average squared deviation from the annual mean.

The analysis was conducted in GeoDa 1.16. Spatial autocorrelation analysis used 30 m fishnet polygon units within the study area. The spatial weights matrix contained 807,583 units, and annual RDSI values were used as the analysis attributes. A spatial weights matrix was constructed using first order queen contiguity, under which units sharing an edge or vertex were defined as neighbours, and the weights were row standardised. Significance was assessed using 999 random permutations, with p≤0.001 used to identify significant local spatial associations. Significant units were classified by comparing their RDSI and spatially lagged neighbouring RDSI with the annual mean. The resulting types were high–high (HH) and low–low (LL) clusters and high–low (HL) and low–high (LH) spatial outliers. All remaining units were classified as not significant.

sec.title: 2.6. Detection of External Driving Factors Using OPGD
sec.p: Mean annual precipitation, mean annual temperature, elevation, soil depth, land use intensity, population density, gross domestic product density, nighttime light, and tourism infrastructure density were selected as explanatory variables for analysing spatial variation in RDSI. Spearman correlation tests and variance inflation factor (VIF) diagnostics were conducted for each year to examine pairwise monotonic correlations and multivariable linear redundancy among the explanatory variables [31]. The joint redundancy screening criteria were |ρ|≥0.8 and VIF≥10. The recurrence of strong correlations across years was also considered when assessing redundancy.

The optimal parameters based geographical detector (OPGD) was used to determine the analytical scale and discretisation scheme for each factor [23,32,33]. Some explanatory variables had a native spatial resolution of 1 km. Analysing external factors directly at 30 m could repeatedly use information from coarser raster cells and produce an overly fine spatial interpretation. Given the relatively limited extent of the study area, the upper candidate grid size was set at 1000 m to balance the identification of spatial differences with sample size requirements within strata. Using 2020 as the reference year, optimal parameters were searched for each factor across grid sizes of 250, 500, 750, and 1000 m. The candidate schemes combined the equal interval, quantile, geometric interval, Fisher–Jenks natural breaks, and standard deviation methods with three to six strata. A common working scale of 1000 m was selected from the mean optimal q value, mean rank, and number of factors attaining their individual maximum q value at each scale. Discretisation parameters were then optimised separately for the five observation years. Each conventional stratum was required to contain at least 30 grids and at least 5% of the total sample. An additional scheme that separated zero values into a distinct stratum was used for variables with a concentration of zero values, and results with insufficient sample support were flagged.

The factor detector used the q statistic to measure the explanatory power of the strata of an explanatory variable for spatial variation in RDSI [34]. (8)q=1−∑h=1LNhσh2Nσ2 where L is the number of strata. N and σ2 are the total sample size and the overall variance in RDSI, respectively, while Nh and σh2 are the sample size and within stratum variance for stratum h. A higher q value indicates stronger explanatory power of the factor strata for spatial variation in RDSI.

Factor significance was assessed using 499 permutations. The candidate discretisation schemes were searched again in every permutation so that parameter optimisation was incorporated into the significance assessment. For the interaction detector, 499 permutations were applied to the selected joint strata. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied separately to the two sets of tests within each year.

Interaction enhancement was identified by comparing the explanatory power of the joint strata, qX1∩X2, with the explanatory power of the two individual factors. Bivariate enhancement was assigned when the joint q value exceeded the larger individual q value but remained below their sum. Nonlinear enhancement was assigned when the joint q value exceeded their sum. The increase in explanatory power, ∆q=qX1∩X2−maxqX1,qX2, was also calculated, and the sample sizes of the joint strata were checked.

The risk detector calculated the mean RDSI and sample size within each optimal stratum of each factor, with an approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean constructed as the mean ± 1.96 times its standard error. Pairwise comparisons between strata were performed using Welch’s t tests, and the resulting p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm method [35]. The four factors with the highest multiyear mean q values were selected to display their 2023 strata. A stratum was labelled as associated with high RDSI when its mean RDSI was at least the study area mean for that year and it either had the highest mean or did not differ significantly from the stratum with the highest mean.

sec.title: 2.7. Tourism Development Potential Assessment
sec.p: A tourism development potential index (TDP) was constructed for 2023 to identify areas with relatively favourable resource attractiveness, transport accessibility, service support and socioeconomic conditions, providing a basis for the spatial organisation of tourism use. Management zoning then combined current rocky desertification sensitivity, recent change and core zone protection constraints to determine conservation and use directions for different areas. Seven indicators were selected according to the characteristics of the study area, the assessment objective, and data availability, with reference to studies on coordination between conservation and tourism in natural World Heritage properties [8], spatial assessment of nature based recreation supply and demand [36], coordination between tourism development and ecological conservation in protected areas [37], and ecotourism suitability assessment [38] (Table 3). Point data for tourist attractions, tourism infrastructure, and public service facilities were converted into continuous density surfaces through kernel density estimation to calculate tourist attraction density (TAD), tourism infrastructure density (TID), and public service facility density (PSFD). These variables represent the spatial concentration of tourism resources and service facilities [39,40]. RDTN is the road network distance to the nearest tourism node, and DTR is the distance to the nearest road. They represent connectivity between tourism nodes and road accessibility. Gross domestic product density (GDP) and population density (PD) were used as proxies for regional economic activity, potential tourism demand, and service support. Because longer distances indicate lower accessibility, RDTN and DTR were treated as negative indicators. The other indicators represented resource attractiveness or socioeconomic support and were treated as positive indicators within the TDP assessment.
Min–max normalisation was used to remove differences in measurement units and align indicator direction. A higher normalised value therefore represents more favourable conditions for tourism use.
Positive indicators were normalised as follows. (9)rij=xij− minxjmaxxj− minxj

Negative indicators were normalised as follows. (10)rij=maxxj−xijmaxxj−minxj where rij and xij are the normalised and original values of indicator j in assessment unit i, respectively. max(xj) and min(xj) are the maximum and minimum values of indicator j among the valid assessment units used for normalisation. For nonconstant indicators, normalised values range from 0 to 1.

A hierarchical weighting method with equal weights among criteria and equal weights among indicators within each criterion was used. TDP provides an integrated comparison of tourism resources and conditions supporting their use. The four assessment criteria were therefore given balanced consideration, without assigning priority to a particular criterion or indicator within a criterion. A score was first calculated for each criterion, after which the four criteria were aggregated with equal weights. This prevents criterion weights from being determined directly by the number of indicators they contain. (11)Dik=1mk∑j∈Jkrij (12)TDPi=∑k=14WkDik, Wk=0.25 where Dik is the score of assessment unit i for criterion k, Jk is the set of indicators in that criterion, mk is the number of indicators, and Wk is the criterion weight. Each of the four criteria was assigned a weight of 0.25. Resource attractiveness contains only TAD, which therefore has a final weight of 0.25. Each of the other three criteria contains two indicators, and each indicator has a final weight of 0.125.

sec.title: 2.8. Management Zoning Rules
sec.p: Management zones were constructed through spatial overlay analysis of current rocky desertification sensitivity, recent class change, and tourism development potential. The 2023 RDSI represented current sensitivity. The insensitive and slightly sensitive classes were combined as low sensitivity, the moderately sensitive class was retained as moderate sensitivity, and the highly and extremely sensitive classes were combined as high sensitivity. Changes in the original five sensitivity class codes from 2020 to 2023 were classified as deterioration, stability, or improvement. Stability and improvement were collectively classified as no deterioration. Tourism development potential was divided into low, moderate, and high levels using natural breaks in the 2023 TDP score distribution, with class breaks of 0.217071 and 0.321304. These levels represent relative differences in tourism resources and conditions supporting their use within the study area and can be combined with the aggregated sensitivity classes for zoning.

The boundaries of the Putao and Lijiang Gorge core zones were merged and rasterised to distinguish the core zones from the buffer zones within the study area. Restoration and prevention needs were first identified from recent change and current sensitivity. Areas of moderate or high sensitivity that recently deteriorated were assigned to the priority restoration zone, while areas of low sensitivity that recently deteriorated were assigned to the risk prevention zone. For areas without deterioration, management direction was further determined from location within the World Heritage property and TDP. All such areas within the core zones were assigned to the conservation maintenance zone. High sensitivity areas in the buffer zones were also assigned primarily to conservation maintenance. Moderate and low sensitivity areas in the buffer zones were further divided among the risk prevention, conservation maintenance, conservation and use coordination, and low disturbance use zones according to tourism development potential. The risk prevention zone addresses two types of prevention need. Low sensitivity areas with recent deterioration require measures to prevent further increases in sensitivity. In buffer zone areas with moderate sensitivity and no deterioration, current sensitivity and low or moderate tourism development potential call for maintaining surface conditions and cautiously planning new uses to prevent new deterioration in sensitivity.

Pixel level logical conditions were applied to the input rasters according to Table 4, producing five mutually exclusive management zones. Sensitivity and recent change were used to determine ecological management needs, the core zones imposed the protection constraint, and tourism development potential further distinguished conservation and use directions within the buffer zones.

sec.title: 3.1. Spatiotemporal Patterns and Class Composition of RDSI
sec.p: Rocky desertification sensitivity declined overall from 2005 to 2023, although it fluctuated among periods (Figure 2). Mean RDSI values for the five observation years were 4.112, 3.937, 4.053, 3.359, and 3.540, respectively. RDSI decreased from 2005 to 2010, increased from 2010 to 2015, declined markedly from 2015 to 2020, and increased slightly from 2020 to 2023. Mean RDSI was 13.91% lower in 2023 than in 2005, indicating an overall reduction in sensitivity despite a recent increase.

Slightly and moderately sensitive areas dominated throughout the study period and together accounted for 90.86% to 94.81% of the study area. In 2005, the moderately sensitive class had the largest area at 339.034 km2, or 46.81%. The slightly sensitive class became dominant after 2010 and expanded to 456.573 km2, or 63.03%, in 2020. From 2005 to 2023, the combined proportion of insensitive and slightly sensitive areas increased from 46.51% to 64.33%, while the combined proportion of highly and extremely sensitive areas decreased from 6.68% to 1.15%. No extremely sensitive pixels were present in 2023. The areas of moderate and high sensitivity increased between 2020 and 2023, consistent with the recent increase in mean RDSI.

Spatially, the sensitivity classes formed a fine patchwork. From 2005 to 2015, moderately and highly sensitive patches occurred mainly in the central north, east, and parts of the central south, with concentrations around Yangdi, Xingping, Baisha, and Putao. By 2020, highly sensitive patches had contracted markedly, while insensitive and slightly sensitive areas had expanded. In 2023, moderately and highly sensitive patches increased again in parts of the central north and central east, although their overall extent remained clearly smaller than in 2005 and 2015.

In 2023, moderately and highly sensitive areas together covered 258.369 km2. Moderately sensitive patches were concentrated in the central north and central east, particularly near Shangshitang and Qingshangen in Baisha Town, Niuling, Gaoling, and Daishang in Yangdi Township, and Damianshan in Xingping Town. Moderately sensitive pixels also occurred near Lijia and Guanzhuang in Dabu Township and Mingcun in Caoping Hui Ethnic Township, with local patches of high sensitivity. In contrast, areas near Guidong and Shuilongshan in Putao Town, Shangendi and Gouheqiao in Nanbianshan Town, and Youziwan in Liutang Town were mainly insensitive or slightly sensitive. Low sensitivity therefore dominated the study area in 2023, although relatively continuous moderately sensitive patches remained in some cone karst depressions.

sec.title: 3.2. RDSI Class Transitions and Recent Changes
sec.p: Class stability was the dominant pattern in every consecutive period and accounted for 60.20% to 77.61% of the study area (Figure 3 and Table 5). From 2005 to 2010, improvement accounted for 16.17%, mainly through transitions from moderate to slight sensitivity and from high to moderate sensitivity. From 2010 to 2015, deterioration increased to 16.20%. Transitions from slight to moderate sensitivity accounted for 9.95%, and those from moderate to high sensitivity accounted for 4.02%. Improvement reached 36.47% from 2015 to 2020, the highest proportion among the four periods, and consisted mainly of transitions from moderate to slight sensitivity and from slight sensitivity to insensitivity. Deterioration increased again to 17.49% from 2020 to 2023. The transition from slight to moderate sensitivity accounted for 13.04% and was the principal deterioration pathway during this period. Most class transitions occurred between adjacent classes, while transitions across two or more classes were relatively uncommon.

Spatially, improved patches from 2005 to 2010 occurred mainly near Duimenling and Damianshan in Xingping Town and Guanzhuang in Dabu Township, while deteriorating patches were more dispersed. Deterioration became more extensive from 2010 to 2015, particularly near Duimenling and Damianshan in Xingping Town and Niuling, Gaoling, and Daishang in Yangdi Township. Improved patches were most widespread from 2015 to 2020 and occurred near Shuilongshan and Guidong in Putao Town, Duimenling and Damianshan in Xingping Town, Guanzhuang in Dabu Township, and Mingcun in Caoping Hui Ethnic Township. Deteriorating patches increased again from 2020 to 2023 and were concentrated near Niuling, Gaoling, and Daishang in Yangdi Township, Mingcun in Caoping Hui Ethnic Township, Guanzhuang and Lijia in Dabu Township, and Shangshitang in Baisha Town. Overall, widespread improvement from 2015 to 2020 was followed by a localised increase in sensitivity from 2020 to 2023. Deteriorating patches in the latter period were used to define recent change in the subsequent management zoning.

sec.title: 3.3. Spatial Clustering of RDSI
sec.p: Global Moran’s I was significantly positive in all five years and ranged from 0.7865 to 0.8149. The pseudo p value from the random permutation test was 0.001 in every year (Table 6), indicating persistently strong positive spatial autocorrelation in RDSI. Moran’s I decreased from 0.8006 in 2005 to 0.7865 in 2015 and then increased to 0.7991 in 2020 and 0.8149 in 2023. Spatial clustering therefore weakened initially and strengthened thereafter. Although mean RDSI was lower in 2023 than in 2005, similar values were more strongly clustered among neighbouring units.

The LISA results further revealed the spatial structure of significant clusters (Figure 4). HH and LL clusters together accounted for 54.61%, 54.29%, 52.04%, 57.88%, and 58.35% of the valid analysis units in 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, and 2023, respectively. This pattern was consistent with the initial decrease and subsequent increase in global Moran’s I. From 2005 to 2015, HH clusters occurred mainly near Shangshitang and Qingshangen in Baisha Town, Duimenling and Damianshan in Xingping Town, and Guanzhuang in Dabu Township. After 2020, HH clustering strengthened around Niuling, Gaoling, and Daishang in Yangdi Township and Mingcun in Caoping Hui Ethnic Township, producing more continuous clusters of high values in the north and central east.

The general locations of LL clusters remained stable. They occurred mainly near Guidong and Shuilongshan in Putao Town, Fuli and Shangfuli in Daxu Town, and Shangendi and Gouheqiao in Nanbianshan Town, with continuous clusters of low values in the west, south, and some river valleys. LH and HL spatial outliers together accounted for less than 0.85% in every year and were scattered mainly along the edges of HH and LL clusters. The local spatial structure of RDSI was therefore dominated by clusters of similar values, and the extent of significant clustering increased after 2015.

sec.title: 3.4. Dominant Sensitivity Components
sec.p: In all five observation years, the spatial pattern of dominant RDSI components was characterised by widespread SLP-dominated areas and local concentrations of FRC-dominated and codominant types (Figure 5). SLP dominated areas had the broadest distribution and formed relatively continuous patches near Niuling, Gaoling, and Daishang in Yangdi Township, Damianshan in Xingping Town, and Lijia in Dabu Township. FRC-dominated areas occurred mainly near Guidong and Shuilongshan in Putao Town, Shangendi and Gouheqiao in Nanbianshan Town, and Youziwan in Liutang Town. The FRC and SLP codominant type formed patches near Shangshitang in Baisha Town. FVC dominated and FRC and FVC codominant areas occurred mainly near Fuli and Shangfuli in Daxu Town and were scattered along some river valleys and depression margins. The overall spatial structure remained stable across the five observation years, and local changes occurred mainly between the SLP-dominated type and FRC-related types.

Area composition was consistent with the spatial pattern (Figure 6a). The SLP-dominated type occupied the largest area in every year, increasing from 50.70% in 2005 to 55.89% in 2023. The FRC-dominated type accounted for 19.60% to 28.32%. Together, these two types covered 71.04% to 82.69% of the study area and formed the main internal sensitivity components. Among the codominant types, the FRC and SLP type accounted for 6.83% to 10.77%, while the FRC and FVC type accounted for 4.26% to 10.28%. The FVC-dominated type accounted for 1.09% to 4.83%, and the remaining types occupied relatively small areas.

Component composition also differed among RDSI classes (Figure 6b). Moderately sensitive areas were consistently dominated by SLP, whose proportion increased from 63.3% in 2005 to 73.6% in 2023. Highly sensitive areas were also dominated by SLP in 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2023, when this type accounted for 59.4% to 71.8%. In 2020, the FRC and SLP codominant type accounted for 50.3%, and the SLP-dominated type for 36.2%. Highly sensitive areas covered only 0.32% of the study area that year, so this compositional change affected a small spatial extent. Extremely sensitive areas in 2005, 2010, and 2015 were dominated by the FRC and SLP codominant type, which accounted for 86.2% to 91.2%. The area of extreme sensitivity fell to 0.0009 km2 in 2020, and no extremely sensitive areas remained in 2023. Thus, moderate and high sensitivity was associated mainly with SLP dominance, whereas early areas of extreme sensitivity were characterised by joint FRC and SLP dominance.

sec.title: 3.5. Redundancy Diagnosis, Scale Effects, and Explanatory Power of Driving Factors
sec.p: The redundancy diagnostics showed no persistent high redundancy among the nine factors. MAT and ELE were the most strongly correlated pair in every year. The absolute values of Spearman’s ρ ranged from 0.679 to 0.703 from 2005 to 2020 and increased to 0.830 in 2023. The maximum VIF ranged from 2.50 to 5.03 and remained below 10 (Table 7). Although MAT and ELE met the high correlation criterion in 2023, they did not simultaneously meet the VIF threshold, and this relationship was not repeated in most years. All nine driving factors were therefore retained for subsequent analysis.

The 2020 scale comparison showed that the mean optimal q value across the nine factors increased with grid size, from 0.070 at 250 m to 0.090 at 500 m, 0.099 at 750 m, and 0.115 at 1000 m. The median increased from 0.058 to 0.102 (Figure 7). At 1000 m, the mean rank was 1.33 and seven of the nine factors attained their maximum q values. Among the four candidate grid sizes of 250, 500, 750, and 1000 m, 1000 m was therefore selected as the common working scale for subsequent analyses of all five observation years.

The optimal discretisation scheme differed among factors. In 2023, the quantile method was selected for MAT, ELE, LUI, PD, GDP, and TID; the equal interval method for MAP, and the Fisher–Jenks natural breaks method for SDEP. For NTL, zero values were placed in a separate stratum before the quantile method was applied. The optimal number of strata ranged from five to six (Table 8). All nine factors were significant in the 499 permutation tests, with BH-adjusted pseudo p values of 0.002.

At the 1000 m working scale, ELE consistently ranked first, while the ranking of the other factors varied among years (Figure 8). ELE had the highest q value in all five years, ranging from 0.293 to 0.410, with a multiyear mean of 0.362. Its strata therefore maintained a strong correspondence with the spatial variation in RDSI. LUI and MAT ranked second and third, with multiyear mean q values of 0.226 and 0.196, respectively, and were among the three highest-ranked factors in every year except 2020. PD had a multiyear mean q value of 0.155. The corresponding values for SDEP, TID, MAP, and GDP were 0.106, 0.100, 0.096, and 0.095. The annual q values of TID, MAP, and GDP did not exceed 0.145.

Interannual changes were not synchronous among the factors. In 2020, ELE remained the highest-ranked factor with a q value of 0.293, followed by PD and MAP. LUI and MAT decreased to their lowest values across the five years, at 0.099 and 0.097, respectively. In 2023, the q values of ELE, MAT, LUI, PD, and SDEP reached 0.409, 0.364, 0.316, 0.279, and 0.267, respectively, all higher than in 2020. SDEP ranged from only 0.037 to 0.102 between 2005 and 2020 but increased to 0.267 in 2023, while PD increased from 0.102 in 2005 to 0.279 in 2023. Thus, strong spatial correspondence in 2023 occurred across factors representing terrain, climate, land use, population, and soil conditions.

NTL had a mean q value of 0.030 across the four years with available results, increasing from 0.001 in 2010 to 0.079 in 2023. The 2005 result was recorded as not available because there were too few nonzero samples, and only 11 positive grids were available in 2010, providing limited support for stratification. Overall, ELE showed consistently high and relatively stable explanatory power, whereas the q values of the other factors varied among years. The q value measures the correspondence between factor strata and the spatial variation in RDSI and does not represent the independent causal contribution of a factor.

sec.title: 3.6. Interactions Among Driving Factors and Strata Associated with High RDSI
sec.p: For every valid pair of factors, the joint q value exceeded the q values of both individual factors, indicating either bivariate or nonlinear enhancement (Figure 9a). Based on the dominant interaction type across the available years, nonlinear enhancement predominated for 20 of the 36 factor pairs and bivariate enhancement for 16 pairs. Across all 172 valid pair-by-year results, bivariate enhancement occurred 89 times and nonlinear enhancement occurred 83 times, showing that both forms of enhancement were common. The eight pairs with the highest mean joint q values all included ELE. MAP and ELE had the highest mean joint q value of 0.465, followed by ELE with LUI, SDEP, GDP, and TID at 0.445, 0.433, 0.431, and 0.426, respectively. Joint stratification involving elevation therefore consistently identified pronounced spatial variation in RDSI.

The ranking by relative gain in explanatory power differed from that by joint q value. Relative to the stronger individual factor, MAP with GDP and MAP with TID each had a mean Δq of 0.128. The corresponding values for MAP with LUI, PD, and SDEP were 0.121, 0.116, and 0.112, respectively (Figure 9b), and valid results were available for all five years. Among pairs without MAP, GDP with TID had the largest mean gain at 0.105. Although MAP with ELE had the highest mean joint q value, its mean gain was 0.103 and ranked seventh. The high absolute explanatory power of pairs containing ELE therefore partly reflected the high individual q value of ELE. In contrast, MAP had relatively low individual explanatory power but produced larger relative gains when jointly stratified with other factors.

Mean RDSI followed different gradients across the 2023 strata of the four main driving factors (Figure 10). Mean RDSI generally decreased as MAT and PD increased. The stratum with MAT no higher than 19.93 °C had a mean RDSI of 4.066, after which mean RDSI generally declined with increasing temperature. The stratum with PD no higher than 26.92 persons km−2 had a mean RDSI of 4.144, the highest among the high RDSI-associated strata for the four factors. Mean RDSI increased with ELE and entered the high RDSI-associated range in the strata from 301.8 to 362.9 m and from 362.9 to 553.4 m. The latter stratum had a mean RDSI of 4.019. Mean RDSI also generally increased with LUI and reached 4.129 in the stratum from 0.9903 to 1.0000. Higher RDSI in 2023 was therefore associated mainly with low temperature, moderate to high elevation, high land use intensity, and low population density.

sec.title: 3.7. Tourism Development Potential and Management Zoning
sec.p: Moderate potential covered the largest area at 371.648 km2, or 51.31%. Low potential covered 311.892 km2, or 43.06%, and high potential covered 40.779 km2, or 5.63% (Figure 11a). Areas of moderate and low potential were widely distributed. High potential occupied a relatively small area and occurred in patches along the western margin and in parts of the central east and south.

Five recommended management zones were delineated according to the rules in Table 4 from the 2023 RDSI class, the RDSI class change from 2020 to 2023, TDP, and core zone protection constraints (Figure 11b and Table 9). The conservation maintenance zone was the largest at 310.250 km2, or 42.83%, and formed relatively continuous areas within the core zones and in the central east. The low disturbance use zone covered 197.648 km2, or 27.29%, and was concentrated mainly in the west and south outside the core zones. The risk prevention and priority restoration zones covered 109.111 km2 and 102.059 km2, or 15.06% and 14.09%, respectively. The risk prevention zone was scattered mainly along the western periphery and the central south and eastern margins. The priority restoration zone was more concentrated around the northern core zone and in the central east and southeast, corresponding to some patches of class deterioration near Yangdi Township, Caoping Hui Ethnic Township, and Dabu Township from 2020 to 2023. The conservation and use coordination zone was the smallest at 5.251 km2, or 0.72%, and occurred as scattered patches around the periphery. The reference patches marked by crosses in Figure 11c illustrate the criteria for the five zoning categories. A core zone patch near Zuohan in Yangdi Township shifted from slight to moderate sensitivity between 2020 and 2023 and was assigned to the priority restoration zone (I), identifying a priority for field verification and assessment of restoration needs. A core zone patch near Yangjia in Xingping Town remained highly sensitive in both years without a class increase and was therefore assigned to the conservation maintenance zone (II). A buffer zone patch near Fengmu’ao in Baisha Town remained moderately sensitive in both years and had low tourism development potential, leading to its assignment to the risk prevention zone (III). A buffer zone patch near Dacunmen in Yangshuo Town also remained moderately sensitive but had high tourism development potential and was assigned to the conservation and use coordination zone (IV). A buffer zone patch near Jiuxian in Baisha Town remained slightly sensitive in both years and had high tourism development potential, leading to its assignment to the low disturbance use zone (V) as a candidate location for subsequent planning of tourism use.

sec.title: 4.1. Sensitivity Patterns Shaped by Surface Cover Change and Terrain
sec.p: Rocky desertification sensitivity in the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site declined overall, but the change was neither continuous nor spatially uniform. Widespread class improvement from 2015 to 2020 coexisted with localised deterioration from 2020 to 2023. The long-term trend must therefore be interpreted together with the direction of change between consecutive periods. Research in South China karst has likewise shown marked spatial heterogeneity in vegetation recovery and associations between recovery pathways, terrain, soil conditions, and changes in rural population [41]. RDSI combines a static slope component with dynamic proxies for surface cover. Changes in FRC and FVC may reflect improved surface conditions, while also being influenced by season, endmember selection, and image quality. For World Heritage management, a decrease in sensitivity is a positive signal, but increases in vegetation cover, soil recovery, and changes in actual bedrock exposure remain distinct processes.

The internal component analysis further showed that declining sensitivity can coexist with persistent terrain constraints. SLP-dominated areas were the most widespread in all five years, indicating that slope retained a relatively high assigned class in most pixels when dominance was defined by the maximum sensitivity score. Because slope was a static component in this study, an increase in the proportion of the SLP-dominated type does not indicate that slope itself changed or that its causal influence strengthened. A possible explanation is that improvements in vegetation cover or changes in rock exposure reduced the sensitivity scores of the corresponding components in some pixels, while the slope score remained unchanged and consequently became the maximum. The small area of the FVC-dominated type therefore does not imply that vegetation change was unimportant to temporal changes in RDSI.

From an ecological perspective, improvement in surface cover may remain constrained by karst geology and by soil and water conditions. A recent review showed that the distinctive connection between surface and subsurface systems in karst regions exposes land degradation processes to the combined influence of geological conditions, land use, and climatic pressure [2]. Lithology-related differences in weathered layer thickness can also affect vegetation productivity through water availability and land–atmosphere feedbacks [42]. Lower RDSI therefore indicates reduced surface sensitivity within the present assessment, but does not necessarily imply concurrent recovery of soil reserves or water regulation. Research in humid karst areas has also shown that revegetation may coincide with decreases in soil moisture and groundwater storage without a corresponding change in regional water yield [43]. Restoration assessments should therefore consider both surface cover and soil and water conditions.

Deterioration covered 17.49% of the study area from 2020 to 2023, and the transition from slight to moderate sensitivity was the principal pathway. Management must therefore consider recent increases within an overall improving trend rather than focusing only on areas in the highest current sensitivity class. Incorporating recent change into zoning allows low sensitivity areas with rising sensitivity to enter preventive management, while the longer transition record provides context for setting inspection frequency and evaluating the continuity of restoration measures.

sec.title: 4.2. Spatial Associations of Terrain, Hydrothermal Conditions, and Land Use and Their Potential Explanations
sec.p: Elevation had the highest spatial explanatory power in all five years, indicating a strong correspondence between elevation strata and spatial variation in RDSI. The internal component analysis also showed that the SLP-dominated type occupied the largest area in every year, reflecting the prominent position of terrain in the composition of sensitivity. Slope is itself a component of RDSI, and elevation and slope may be spatially associated. The q value for elevation may therefore also contain information about its spatial co-distribution with slope and related surface conditions. This study has not quantified the specific influence of this association, so the high q value for elevation cannot be interpreted directly as an independent causal contribution. From an ecological perspective, terrain and soil rock structure in karst regions can influence water infiltration, runoff redistribution and soil retention [42,44]. These processes may help explain the correspondence between elevation strata and spatial differences in sensitivity.

In addition to terrain, land use intensity and mean annual temperature showed relatively strong associations with spatial variation in RDSI. LUI had the second highest multiyear mean q value, and higher LUI strata in 2023 corresponded to higher mean RDSI, indicating differences in sensitivity under different land use conditions. Studies of karst hillslopes suggest that vegetation cover, land use and rainfall conditions may jointly influence surface runoff and soil erosion [45]. The associations of MAT and SDEP may reflect spatial differences in the thermal and soil moisture conditions required for vegetation growth [46]. Research in Bijie found that land use and population density became important explanatory factors during the later study period [4]. This study also found that lower population density strata in 2023 corresponded to higher RDSI. This may be related to spatial associations among population distribution, terrain constraints and land use patterns, but does not establish that population decline increases rocky desertification sensitivity. The relationship between population change and vegetation recovery may also vary with regional socioeconomic and land use conditions [41].

MAP had relatively low explanatory power as an individual factor, but its combination with ELE produced the highest mean joint q value. This indicates that the joint stratification of precipitation and elevation identifies more pronounced spatial differences in RDSI and that the influence of precipitation may vary with terrain. Precipitation supplies water for vegetation growth, while terrain and soil rock structure affect water retention, infiltration, and convergence. Once runoff forms, erosion also depends on slope cover and soil condition. Observations in Southwest China karst show that rainfall-driven runoff and erosion are jointly regulated by slope, soil moisture, and vegetation [47]. Regional vegetation research has also identified strong joint explanatory power for actual evapotranspiration and elevation [46]. These findings offer a possible explanation of the interaction pattern in terms of water input and terrain-controlled redistribution. The large gains in explanatory power for MAP combined with LUI, GDP and TID also suggest joint associations between precipitation strata and different land use or socioeconomic spatial patterns that warrant further investigation. Research in Chongqing karst found a strong combined influence of precipitation and vegetation cover on changes in soil erosion [5], consistent with the joint roles of moisture conditions and land use indicated here. Overall, spatial variation in RDSI may be shaped by terrain-related habitat differences, hydrothermal regulation of vegetation, and land use effects on surface cover.

sec.title: 4.3. Implications of Zoning for Sustainable Management of the World Heritage Property
sec.p: This study combined current sensitivity, recent change, tourism development potential and core zone protection constraints to delineate five recommended management zones and identify priorities for conservation, prevention and use in different areas. The zoning results are intended primarily to inform subsequent field verification and management decisions. Their actual management effectiveness requires further examination through continued monitoring and independent evaluation after measures have been implemented. Naturally steep slopes, exposed rock, and tower and cone karst landscapes in the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site have important conservation value. A high RDSI does not necessarily indicate a need for active restoration. Specific measures should be determined from landform characteristics and actual degradation, with the conservation of natural landforms and the integrity of the property as prerequisites.

Management of the conservation maintenance zone should focus on retaining vegetation cover, soil stability, and landscape integrity. Continuous high sensitivity patches and their surroundings should be incorporated into routine patrols, with controls on new surface disturbance. In the priority restoration zone, recently deteriorating patches with relatively high current sensitivity should first be checked to establish actual degradation and restoration needs. Enclosure for natural regeneration, natural recovery or necessary local soil and water conservation measures should then be selected according to surface conditions. Specific interventions should be based on field-confirmed degradation, with the conservation of natural landforms and landscape integrity as prerequisites. Low disturbance measures such as enclosure and the promotion of natural recovery should be prioritised within the core zones. Naturally steep slopes and exposed rock landscapes with heritage value should retain their natural forms, and restoration measures should target locations where field verification establishes a need. Measures in the risk prevention zone should address different prevention needs. In low sensitivity areas that have recently deteriorated, surface cover monitoring and field verification should be strengthened, and sources of disturbance should be controlled promptly. In buffer zone areas with moderate sensitivity, no deterioration and low or moderate tourism development potential, management should maintain vegetation cover and soil stability and cautiously plan new roads, facilities and uses to prevent increases in sensitivity.

Tourism activities should preferentially use existing roads, service facilities, and suitable activity spaces within the low disturbance use zone. Consolidating visitor routes, concentrating stopping points, and maintaining established trails can reduce vegetation trampling and the expansion of bare ground caused by dispersed access. Research in protected areas has shown that informal trail networks can cause vegetation loss and soil erosion and that their management needs to consider environmental conditions and route characteristics [48]. Trail width, vegetation damage, and changes in bare ground can therefore be monitored and used to adjust the area and intensity of tourism activities. In this way, the resource and service advantages represented by TDP can support low-disturbance use.

The conservation and use coordination zone can provide a focus for residents, tourism operators, and management agencies to develop shared rules for routes, facility locations, and ecological maintenance. Research in national parks has shown that differences in stakeholder preferences for ecosystem services affect the formation of landscape use conflicts [28]. Residents’ livelihood needs and visitor activity patterns can therefore be considered when coordinating uses that overlap spatially, and monitoring results can inform subsequent adjustments. Clear priorities for each zone, together with negotiated rules for use, can translate sensitivity assessment into practical measures that address World Heritage conservation, community needs, and tourism.

sec.title: 4.4. Limitations and Future Work
sec.p: This study used multisource data for five observation years to characterise changes among periods, but the observation frequency limits the identification of continuous interannual fluctuations and short-term disturbances. Differences among sensors, image compositing and FVC and FRC endmember settings may affect comparisons across years, and the direction of the small mean RDSI change during 2010–2015 remains uncertain. Future work should use consistent products and processing where possible, with sensor harmonisation and consistent observation windows when combining historical imagery. Static soil depth and differences in the coverage of socioeconomic and POI data may also affect comparisons of external factors. Updated soil measurements and historical records with consistent spatial and temporal coverage would improve these comparisons.

Spatial results may vary with grid size, statistical stratification and the definition of neighbours. OPGD grids were limited to 250–1000 m within the study area of 724.319 km2. Coarser grids would reduce the number of analytical units and could obscure local differences or provide insufficient samples within strata. Future studies could extend scale comparisons to larger study areas while maintaining adequate sample support and examine whether the factor associations persist.

The management zones are recommendations derived from sensitivity scores, recent change and conditions for tourism use. Their stability under alternative input data, weights and classification settings has not been systematically evaluated. Future analyses should compare zone areas, boundaries and assignment agreement across alternative settings. The zoning also lacks a separate constraint for naturally exposed bedrock and geomorphological features requiring conservation, so some priority restoration patches may contain features that should remain in their natural state. Representative satellite images provide qualitative context but cannot independently validate sensitivity classes or management zones. Field surveys and independent reference data should distinguish actual degradation from natural landscapes and inform the addition of geomorphological conservation constraints. Land tenure, visitor routes, facilities and community needs could then help refine operational management units and support subsequent updates.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: From 2005 to 2023, rocky desertification sensitivity in the Guilin Karst World Natural Heritage Site showed an overall decline, periodic increases, and persistent spatial clustering. Mean RDSI decreased from 4.112 to 3.540. Improvement was most extensive from 2015 to 2020, whereas 17.49% of the study area deteriorated from 2020 to 2023. Moran’s I ranged from 0.7865 to 0.8149, and high and low RDSI values remained strongly clustered throughout the study period. The decline in RDSI indicates reduced sensitivity within the present assessment framework, but does not imply simultaneous recovery of soil and hydrological conditions.

The internal component analysis showed that SLP-dominated and FRC-dominated types together accounted for 71.0% to 82.7% of the study area, reflecting the prominent roles of slope and rock cover in the composition of sensitivity. At the common 1000 m working scale, ELE had the highest individual explanatory power in every year, with a multiyear mean q value of 0.362. LUI and MAT ranked next. MAP and ELE had the highest mean joint q value of 0.465. These results show persistent terrain stratification in the spatial variation in RDSI, together with strong joint associations involving land use and hydrothermal conditions.

This study incorporated sensitivity class changes from 2020 to 2023 into management zoning, delineating five recommended management zones based on current sensitivity, tourism development potential and core zone protection constraints. The approach distinguishes recently deteriorating and non-deteriorating units within the same sensitivity class and identifies spatial priorities for prevention, field verification and assessment of restoration needs. Specific management measures still need to be determined from actual degradation and the conservation requirements of the World Heritage property. These zoning criteria can inform differentiated management in comparable karst protected areas.
